summary: Marvis is a helmet HUD for Mars surface exploration, with a Meta Quest 3 standing in for the visor. Its first strength is that it never asks a gloved hand to press anything. Thick spacesuit gloves make touchscreens and small buttons impractical, so every control works by palm gesture and voice alone: an open left palm raises the 3D map, a fist unfolds it or arms the SOS, and the right hand points and pinches from a distance to pick places and operate menus. Waypoints are named by speaking. Its second strength is a route that stays alive. The route starts from NASA orbiter terrain data, then the helmet’s depth sensor reads the ground about 4 m ahead five times a second, marks obstacles and drops deeper than 0.3 m, and redraws the route around them at once. It prefers ground already seen over unseen ground, and switches to a return-to-base route when the suit’s readings turn dangerous.
details:
The problem and our answer. An astronaut on foot on Mars needs one map of the exact ground under their boots, and must read and control it in thick gloves. Orbital maps were built for regional views: across our 2 km site the sharpest image resolves about 0.64 m per pixel, so a rock at your feet is invisible from orbit. Marvis is a helmet heads-up display that starts from NASA data, fills in what orbit cannot see with sensors of its own, and is operated without touching anything. A Meta Quest 3 headset stands in for the visor.

How it works. Data from four NASA Mars missions (MRO, Mars Odyssey, MGS and the Curiosity rover) is layered into one 3D map of the Gediz Vallis channel in Gale Crater, where Curiosity found pure sulfur in 2024. The map appears above the open left palm and switches between elevation, slope, optical and night thermal layers. A route from base to the survey site is computed from the slope of the terrain. The field map then zooms in to the ground around the wearer and overwrites the NASA map with what the helmet’s depth sensor sees: obstacles and drops deeper than 0.3 m are marked on a grid of 10 cm cells several times a second, and whenever the grid changes the route is planned again and redrawn as arrows on the real floor. The planner prefers ground already seen over unseen ground and can pass through waypoints the astronaut sets and names by voice. Survival readings, among them the radiation, air pressure and temperature Curiosity measured at this site, stay beside the line of sight as tiles ranked by importance, and when a reading turns critical the view turns red, a spoken alert plays and the route switches to return to base.

Impact. The aim is safer, more self-reliant surface exploration. A crew gets one view of the place they are walking, built from what orbiters and rovers already know, honest about where that knowledge stops, and able to take over from there. Hands stay free for tools and samples, and everything, speech recognition included, runs on the suit’s own computer with no internet connection, which matters on a planet with no network.

Creativity. Two ideas set the project apart. First, the interface is never touched: an open palm raises the map, a fist unfolds it or arms the SOS, the right hand points and pinches from a distance to pick places and press menu buttons, and short spoken commands do the rest. Second, the NASA map corrects itself in real space: a route planned from orbit bends around a rock the orbiter could not see. We also carried these ideas through to working hardware instead of leaving them as a concept. The ambient temperature on the HUD, for example, is measured by a real temperature sensor on an Arduino and read once a second by the suit computer, so when the surroundings run too hot the alert and the return-to-base route are triggered by a real measurement.

Validity. The route is checked against ground truth: Curiosity drove 593 m between the same two points, and our walking route is 390 m long, climbs 45 m and never crosses ground steeper than 14.9°. Ground steeper than 20° is closed, a limit taken from Apollo and Artemis walking experience. The data layers pass 56 automated checks, including cross-checks against Curiosity’s own record, and the planners, the hand pointer and the alert logic have automated tests. We state the limits plainly: the slope limits come from the Moon, on our headset the live scan reached about 2.5 m around the wearer.

Relevance. The challenge, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, asks for a layered view from multiple NASA missions, a route that avoids obstacles, attention to astronaut safety and to how a spacesuit limits mobility, and suggests a HUD on the helmet visor. Each has a direct answer here: four missions and five kinds of data (topographic, optical, thermal, radiation, atmospheric) in one map, a slope-based route that is planned again around scanned obstacles, live alerts with a return-to-base route, glove-free control, and a working HUD.

Tools. Headset app: JavaScript, Three.js, WebXR (hand tracking, depth sensing, mesh and plane detection, anchors) and Vite, on a Meta Quest 3. Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow and Requests. Suit hub: Python with aiohttp, pySerial and sherpa-onnx, running the Silero VAD, SenseVoice and Supertonic 3 speech models on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super. Sensor: an Arduino Mega 2560 with a temperature sensor, read over USB serial.

Factors we considered. Glove mobility, astronaut safety first, the resolution limit of orbital data, human walking slope limits, tracing every value on screen back to NASA data or a real sensor, marking simulated readings as simulated, and keeping the view uncluttered. In our demo a room stands in for a scaled-down patch of Mars, with a chair playing the rock.
